body: What would be interesting to know is how many developers encounter this problem (e.g., questions asked on Stack Overflow) and if there are popular libraries that provide workarounds (should be fairly easy to prototype with `input.files[0].size` et al).

* https://stackoverflow.com/q/3717793/441757 has 232 upvotes, [13 duplicates](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/linked/3717793?lq=1) 
* https://stackoverflow.com/q/5697605/441757 has 54 upvotes, [3 duplicates](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/linked/5697605?lq=1)

> (should be fairly easy to prototype with `input.files[0].size` et al).

The question with 232 upvotes has an answer at https://stackoverflow.com/a/3717847/441757 with 302 upvotes that uses `input.files[0].size`.

> if there are popular libraries that provide workarounds 

That question with 232 upvotes also has an answer with 110 upvotes which provides a solution that relies on jQuery. The most-upvoted answers to the other two questions listed above also have solutions that rely on jQuery.
@smaug---- @tkent-google @rniwa thoughts on this? I guess in particular for "maximum size of all selected files" per the above data.

It would be a bit weird to have validation message if user selects too large file.
I wonder if it is possible to pass max size to OS level file pickers and then users couldn't even select too large files. (didn't immediately see anything on gtk's filepicker)

> It would be a bit weird to have validation message if user selects too large file.
> I wonder if it is possible to pass max size to OS level file pickers and then users couldn't even select too large files. (didn't immediately see anything on gtk's filepicker)

 For macOS, I can't recall ever having seen any behavior in the filepicker that prevents me from picking particular files based on size. Same for Android.

Regardless, at the spec level, I wouldn't think we could assume the user is on a device/platform/OS with a filepicker that can limit selection to files below a certain size.

The validation message can be the fallback (and either we wouldn't expose the `File` object). If developers are otherwise writing their own validation message ours wouldn't be less weird and over time it could be improved by better file pickers.

few ideas:

use existing min/max attribute for controlling how many files you can pick

- `type="file" multiple min="2" max="2"` require a front & back side for a double-sided print
- `type="file" multiple max="5"` don't allow more then 5 image for a slideshow 

allow controlling byte size

- `type="file" multiple max-file-size="1024"`
- `type="file" multiple total-max-size="1024"`
  - must use bytes, not KB, KiB or any other measurement unit, 1024 vs 1000 is confusing as it already is.
  - should not have to use decimals if you want really small size limits

maybe it also would be useful do ignore junk files by disallow empty/small files so a `min size` would be useful as well?

Any progress? I think changing spec to allow `maxlength` for <input type=file> and using bytes for the length would be the best way forward.

The only detail that needs to be decided is `maxlength` combined with `multiple`. I think the `maxlength` should be total bytes combined instead of per file selected. If both cases need to be handled, then having something like `maxfilesize` (bytes) and `maxsubmissionsize` (bytes) would be a better option.
I wonder if @hober @cdumez @mfreed7 @whatwg/forms have thoughts here?

I'd vote against `maxlength` - while that's a known term in networking and server side nomenclature, it means very little semantically from an HTML perspective. Using a semantic names like `max-file-size` and `max-input-size` make their usage clear.

also while uploading file how much files should be selected,
for now we have to use javascript but it is good to have it  in html

Simplicity and convenience should prevail. Solutions in JS either use several lines or are code-dependent and error-prone. Caution should be observed with Stackoverflow votes. Even if the solution tend to be the simplest ones, the answerers are less prone to question the standards than it should be done here.

Beyond coding verbosity, the main argument against a max file size attribute is that the verification should be performed on server-side. However, input types and attributes that constraint input values already exist (number min max and step, date, email, etc.). Any non beginner developer would perform the check on both client and server sides, no matter the type of input.

Moreover, a lack of coding a client-side size limit should be counterproductive (especially for a file upload) if such a limit exists on the server-side. A too big upload operation should be blocked the sooner as possible and thus preserve the bandwidth (we should avoid carrying a fridge to the recycling center if the recycling center won't accept it...)

Another potential benefit is that for image upload inputs like `<input type="file" accept="image/jpeg" max-file-size="1024">` user-agents could offer to automatically shrink an image that doesn't fit. Like how some of them already use other validation attributes as UI hints, such as opening a numeric keypad for `<input type="text" pattern="[0-9]+">`

Of course the max size can be controlled with JS, just like the mime type via `blob.type`.

But if the `<input>` allows to control the mime type with the `accept` attribute (see example below) it only seems logical there should be an attribute to also control for the max size of the selected file.

```
<input type="file" accept="image/jpeg,image/jpg,image/png">
```

As it is, it seems as if the `<input>` is actually incomplete regarding file selection...

@annevk: 
> What would be interesting to know is how many developers encounter this problem (e.g., questions asked on Stack Overflow) and if there are popular libraries that provide workarounds (should be fairly easy to prototype with `input.files[0].size` et al).

But it seems nice and consistent if we can declaratively in the HTML set a maxsize attribute for a single file.

Would be interesting to know how to specify with this attribute for multiple files.

Obviously none of this is a substitute for server validation as people could generate HTTP requests to submit the multipart data outside of a browser.

Maybe all these can be valid:

```html
<input type=file maxsize=1024Kb>
<input type=file maxsize=1MB>
<input type=file maxsize=1mib>
<input type=file maxsize=32kb>
```

Nightmare to choose between [SI and trad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byte#Multiple-byte_units) units tho.

> could generate HTTP requests to submit the multipart

I proposed in https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/issues/1130 that multipart payloads should also include more headers in each entry so that you can validate more early how big files are on the server and close the connection earlier if something is too big.

> > could generate HTTP requests to submit the multipart
> 
> I proposed in [whatwg/fetch#1130](https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/issues/1130) that multipart payloads should also include more headers in each entry so that you can validate more early how big files are on the server and close the connection earlier if something is too big.

@jimmywarting seems like a nice idea, but I just meant people could send whatever files they wanted to a server to side-step any client-side validation. 

If we implement your idea, I think it will stop that. 

But it's a long way off, and many servers will continue to use the old (then, but current now) multipart format without your headers for a long time. And even the new format will probably try to be backwards compatible (HTML style of accepting many inputs, [generous with what you accept](https://devopedia.org/postel-s-law)), and will accept the old 'headerless' multipart uploads to accommodate older clients, providing a way to side-step its intent, so your "rule" may not end up doing much at all. 

Anyway, it's a cool thing, but it can't help fix it yet as it's not implemented, and it may not do anything at all because of backwards compatibility.

**The attribute name should not mention "file"** The attribute for an image width is "width", not "image-width": `` Similarly, given that "file" primarily appears in the type attribute, the max size attribute for a file should be kept shortest as possible and not mention "file" in its name: `` **The attribute unit should be just bytes** In my opinion, allowing for different units (1MB, mib) can be fuel for debate that can impede the development of this great feature. It can still be added in future implementations while being compatible with just-in-bytes values. **Suggestions** Even if HTML already defines attributes such as `minlength` and `maxlength` (no dashes). I have a little preference for the naming with a `-` that gives a better readability. ``` ``` ``` ```
